422: ///
423: /// [`kontor_runtime_codex`] is not composed here, and the reason is structural
424: /// rather than an omission. Its production account authority
425: /// (`CodexPinnedAccounts`) borrows a store, an `AccountResolver` — itself bound to
426: /// a resolver policy of approved config homes and keychain targets — and the
427: /// fleet's availability boundary. This daemon has no configuration surface for
428: /// any of those, and the borrows cannot outlive the single private store
429: /// connection [`kontor_api::state::ApiState`] owns. Wiring it means giving the
430: /// credential policy a configuration surface, which belongs with the account and
431: /// CLI work rather than here. Until then a Codex plane is composed by its own
432: /// caller and handed in through [`RuntimeRegistry`], which is exactly the seam
433: /// this function uses.
434: ///

1: //! Approved credential references, and the short-lived environment they resolve
2: //! into.
3: //!
4: //! # Why a profile cannot name a path
5: //!
6: //! The obvious design is to let a profile store the directory or keychain entry
7: //! its credentials live in. That makes the profile table a place where writing a
8: //! row is equivalent to reading an arbitrary file, and it makes `..`, symlink
9: //! traversal and prefix confusion into live attack surface reachable from
10: //! whatever creates profiles.
11: //!
12: //! So a profile stores an *alias*, and a [`ResolverPolicy`] — built in memory at
13: //! composition time from trusted local operator configuration — is the only
14: //! thing that maps an alias to something real. Profile input never participates
15: //! in path joining: the policy canonicalizes each approved directory once, at
16: //! build time, and resolution is an exact lookup of an already-canonical path.
17: //! There is no join, so there is nothing for `..` to escape.
18: //!
19: //! # Why the resolved value has no serialized form
20: //!
21: //! [`ResolvedAccountEnvironment`] has private fields, no `Serialize`, and
22: //! `Debug`/`Display` that print variable *names* and a redaction marker. The
23: //! single exit is [`ResolvedAccountEnvironment::apply`], which writes into a
24: //! [`std::process::Command`]'s environment block. That is a deliberate choice of
25: //! mechanism, not a convenience: `std::env::set_var` would make the value
26: //! process-global and visible to every other resolution, a command flag or a
27: //! prompt would put it in argv where any local process can read it, and a shell
28: //! fragment would make quoting a security property.
29: //!
30: //! # Why errors carry codes
31: //!
32: //! A keychain error's `Display` can name the service and account it failed on; a
33: //! filesystem error's can contain the path. Both identify a user. Every failure
34: //! below is therefore mapped to a [`ResolutionReason`] *at the boundary*, and no

10: //! request and posts `asma/publication-identity` for it.
11: //!
12: //! Everything here is inert until an operator installs the App and writes
13: //! `<state root>/config/github-app.json`. Absent configuration is valid; a
14: //! present document that will not parse refuses the start, as the quota-signal
15: //! document does. The private key is read from a path the document names and
